title: Interview with Elder Jim Blizzard
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro

outline.title: Personal Testimony and Background
subpoints: Growing up in a pastor's home
Early struggle with defining a conversion moment

outline.title: The Call to Ministry
subpoints: Initial reluctance due to witnessing pastoral hurt
Recognition of the need for biblical pastors
Support from spouse in pursuing seminary

outline.title: Current Ministry Context
subpoints: Serving an aging congregation in Cape Canaveral
Challenges of transient population and geography
Commitment of the local church to God's Word

outline.title: Observations on Evangelicalism
subpoints: Growth in numbers but dilution of doctrine
Rise of 'church hurt' and religious trauma
Shift in cultural attitudes toward church attendance

summary:
In this afternoon interview, Pastor Tito Lyro sits down with Elder Jim Blizzard to discuss his journey into the ministry and the current state of the church. Elder Blizzard shares his personal testimony, noting that while he grew up in a pastor's home and does not recall a specific moment of conversion, he has always trusted in Christ as his Savior. He reflects on the challenges of growing up in ministry, including the pain of seeing his father face congregational conflicts, which initially deterred him from pursuing the pastorate.

The conversation shifts to the broader evangelical landscape, highlighting a significant shortage of qualified pastors willing to teach the Bible faithfully. Blizzard cites statistics from the North American Reformed Presbyterian Council regarding empty pulpits and the decline of students entering pastoral tracks. He describes his own call to ministry as a gradual realization of the need for biblically grounded leaders who are actively engaged in their communities.

Blizzard also provides insight into his current role at Grace Church in Cape Canaveral, Florida. He describes the congregation as aging and deeply committed to the Gospel, yet facing challenges due to the transient nature of the local population and geographic barriers. The discussion concludes with observations on modern evangelicalism, noting a trend toward watered-down doctrine and the increasing prevalence of 'church hurt' and religious trauma as cultural phenomena.
